source.title: Interpolation and Learning with Scale Dependent Kernels
source.authors: Nicolò Pagliana; Alessandro Rudi; E. De Vito; L. Rosasco

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Minor formula and PDF-text formatting artifacts do not prevent reading it.
record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes and experimentally measures excess risk as sample size changes for minimum-norm interpolating kernel estimators. This is a conceptual test of the more-data version, using kernels rather than the original deep-network settings; it does not locate a finite interpolation threshold.
record.gate_note: The paper cites double-descent work but those cited results are not its own. Its own sample-size results relevant to V3 are recorded below. The smallest-eigenvalue and excess-risk-versus-scale plots (Figures 1 and 2) do not measure a claim version. No model-size or epoch sweep is reported.
record.test_reason: The study derives bounds and runs small simulations on minimum-norm interpolating kernel regression with scale-dependent Matérn/Laplace kernels. These estimators interpolate at every sample size. There is no finite interpolation threshold, and no sweep over model size, epochs or capacity across that threshold. The sample-size result (error falls, then plateaus; the fixed-γ upper bound eventually rises) concerns consistency of interpolating estimators in fixed dimension, not the double-descent peak. It does not show the 'more data hurts near the interpolation threshold' effect V3 names. The original Belkin et al. work appears only as motivating citation [5].
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is essentially right. The authors conclude that ridgeless kernel regression error decreases while n is below exponential in d, then flattens, preventing consistency. This is driven by point separation and the smallest eigenvalue of the kernel matrix. Tuning the kernel scale improves stability and keeps variance bounded.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes minimum-norm interpolants with scale-dependent Matérn kernels and uses Laplace kernels in its numerical experiments. It does not reproduce deep-network size, epoch, or interpolation-threshold sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that kernel scale γ changes stability and variance; the numerical excess-risk behavior depends on the chosen scale. The experiment uses d=10 and a single stated regression and noise setup.

fits_no_version.finding: For ridgeless Laplace/Matérn kernel interpolants in fixed dimension d=10, excess risk falls with n, then plateaus (Fig. 3). The fixed-γ variance bound grows once n exceeds a level exponential in d. Tuning γ≈n^{-2/d} keeps variance bounded but gives no consistency.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Minimum-norm kernel interpolants in fixed dimension are stable only while n is sub-exponential in d; beyond that their error stops improving (no consistency), and kernel scale controls the variance.

record.problems: The numerical evidence is described as a basic experiment, averages 20 simulations, and evaluates on a validation set of 10³ data; no uncertainty bars are stated. The reported sample-size experiment uses one dimension and one regression/noise setup and does not identify a finite interpolation threshold. The theoretical increase is an upper-bound trend, not an observed error increase.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant results omitted. Figures 1 and 2 concern the kernel-matrix smallest eigenvalue and excess risk versus scale, respectively, rather than the claim versions' size, epoch, or sample-size risk curves.

untested.parts: No model-size sweep or deep-network test-error curve.
No interpolation threshold exists for these estimators; no sample sweep near such a threshold.
No capacity sweep past an interpolation point.
No effective-complexity predictor of peak location.
Noise variance is bounded and fixed; no noise sweep, multiple peaks or tuned ridge regularization.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' with a V3 limits_scope verdict is withdrawn. The study is about benign interpolation and consistency in kernel ridgeless regression, not about the double-descent curve. Numerical evidence is figure-only, with 20 simulations and no error bars.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size sweep or deep-network test-error curve.
The study does not locate or sweep around a finite interpolation threshold; its kernel estimators interpolate for each sample set.
No capacity sweep across model classes or risk curve past an interpolation point.
No test of whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and samples.
Noise variance is assumed bounded and used in the analysis, but noise dependence, multiple peaks, and optimally tuned regularization are not tested.
No comparison with an effective parameter count or test of whether such a count turns a second descent into a U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: minimum-norm interpolating estimator f†_{γ,z} with Laplace kernel
rows.operation_detail: Varied training sample size n and measured excess risk for fixed kernel scale γ.

conditions.value: fixed γ; specific values are figure only
average of 20 simulations on a validation set of 10³ data

rows.measure: Approximation of excess risk as a function of n
rows.value: For any fixed γ, excess error decreases with n and then reaches a constant value.
rows.note: The paper describes the trend in the text but gives no plotted numerical values in the text. The reported trend is a decrease followed by a plateau, not an increase. The sample-size sweep is not positioned relative to a finite interpolation threshold.
rows.check: The Fig. 3 sample-size sweep uses an always-interpolating kernel estimator with no interpolation threshold. A decrease-then-plateau in n cannot show or refute V3's rise near the threshold. The 'absent' state wrongly implies a test of V3.

rows.subject: minimum-norm interpolating estimator f†_{γ,z} with scale-dependent Matérn kernels
rows.operation_detail: Derived a sample-size-dependent upper bound on expected excess risk, including a regime where the bound starts increasing for fixed γ.

conditions.value: Assumptions 1–3; well-specified model and bounded output variance

rows.measure: Theoretical upper bound on expected excess risk
rows.baseline: For n≤Ns,d, the stated bound decreases with n for the specified smoothness regime.
rows.value: For n>Ns,d, the bound for fixed γ starts to increase with n; the text also states that tuning γ can keep the variance bounded while the error plateaus.
rows.locator: Sections 3.2–3.3, Theorems 1–2 and discussion of Proposition 1
rows.note: An increasing upper bound does not establish that the realized or expected test error increases. The bound concerns expected excess risk, not an observed rise in the numerical experiment.
rows.check: This is a theoretical upper bound that rises with n for fixed γ when n exceeds N_{s,d} (exponential in d). It concerns loss of stability as points crowd together, not a sample-wise peak at an interpolation threshold. A bound increase is not an observed error increase.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
